newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-IMF team warns Czechs against fast rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-IMF team warns Czechs against fast rate cuts.

text.p: An International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission to the Czech Republic called on Thursday for interest rates to be lowered carefully to prevent a further weakening of the crown.

Analysts said the IMF team's statement, issued after talks with senior government, central bank and labour union officials, was a boost to the central bank in its policy of keeping rates high to protect the crown.

"(The mission) stressed... the necessity for a careful approach to lowering interest rates so that there would not be an undesirable weakening of the crown exchange rate," IMF Czech representative Jiri Jonas said in a statement.
The IMF team came to Prague earlier this month in the wake of turmoil on the foreign exchange market which led to a central bank decision to float the crown on May 27.
The Czech National Bank sharply raised rates before the float in an effort to stem speculative crown short-selling.

"The IMF saying that was a big boost for the central bank. The bank wants to prioritise the currency, it doesn't want to lower interest rates too quickly and the IMF saying that gives them a bit of credibility," said Matt Starr, head of capital martkets at Creditanstalt in Prague.
The central bank has since gradually eased rates on its open market operations but many analysts say a further relaxation of rates and liquidity could lead to another weakening of the crown.
The central bank's repo rate has come down to 25 percent from a peak of 75 percent and the market has been awaiting a lowering of the last resort Lombard facility from its current 50 percent.

"It looks as if the interest rates are going to continue to be very high and that is obviously not the best thing for growth," Starr said, adding it could take three to six months for rates to fall to pre-crisis levels.
The IMF statement followed better-than-expected figures for economic growth, which showed gross domestic product grew 1.5 percent in the first quarter.
Starr said this would give the CNB room to keep policy tight.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, whose government won a razor-thin vote of confidence in parliament last week, said on Tuesday that high interest rates were depressing the economy and that growth this year would be very low.

"(The IMF statement) is hidden support for the calls from the central bank for a very restrictive fiscal policy. It might be support for the central bank against the government," said analyst Vladimir Kreidl of Patria Finance.
In the wake of the crown float, the government announced a package of spending cuts which, with an earlier such package, will cut 45.5 billion crowns from this year's budget.
The mission described the restrictive measures as steps in the right direction. Kreidl said this could be understood as a call for deeper cuts.
Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said on Wednesday the government aims for a 10 billion crown state budget surplus in 1998. "That is not the courage that we need at the moment," Kreidl said.

The statement said the IMF team, CNB governor Josef Tosovksy and finance ministry officials agreed to continue dialogue to evaluate the restrictive steps taken and, if necessary, to formulate further steps to correct imbalances in the economy.
